dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — אֲרוּחַת עֶרֶב בְּיוֹם שִׁשִּׁי
dialogs.intro: Noa invites Budi to Shabbat dinner at her family's home.

lines.speaker: נֹעָה:
lines.id: Budi, will you come over on Friday?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: I'd love to! What's the occasion?

lines.speaker: נֹעָה:

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: אָז אָבִיא יַיִן. זֶה מִנְהָג אֶצְלֵנוּ.

lines.speaker: נֹעָה:
lines.id: That's so sweet. Come at seven?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:

lines.text: בֶּטַח. וְאַל תִּדְאַג, אַבָּא מְדַבֵּר אַנְגְּלִית.

notes: ⚠️ **Hebrew has its own imperative, but Israelis more often use the FUTURE.** תָּבוֹא ("you will come") is used for "come", תִּשְׁלְחִי for "send". This isn't laziness — the future sounds **softer** than a direct command, much like English "will you come?" instead of "come!".

**The true imperative is still used for common verbs and short commands**: בּוֹא (come), לֵךְ (go), קַח (take), תֵּן (give), שֵׁב (sit). You need to recognize them, because you'll hear all five every day.
**"Don't" always uses אַל + future**, never the imperative: אַל תָּבִיא (don't bring). Hebrew has no negative imperative at all.

**כְּלוּם** (*klum*) = "nothing". It's used with a negative: אַל תָּבִיא כְּלוּם, לֹא רָאִיתִי כְּלוּם. Unlike standard English, the two negatives don't cancel out — like "I didn't see nothing", but perfectly correct.
**בְּשִׂמְחָה** ("with joy") is the warmest way to accept an invitation. Other options: בְּכֵיף, בְּוַדַּאי, אֶשְׂמַח מְאוֹד.
⚠️ **אֵלֵינוּ** = "to our place". The base word is אֶל (to), which takes endings like other prepositions: אֵלַי, אֵלֶיךָ, אֵלָיו, אֵלֶיהָ, אֵלֵינוּ. The same ending machine, for the fifth time.
**בְּדִיּוּק** (*bedi'uk*) = "exactly, precisely". On its own it means "exactly!" — a reply you'll often hear when you guess something right.

**Friday-night dinner** is the most valuable invitation you can get in Israel. If you're invited, come on time, bring something small (wine, cake or flowers), and be ready to eat far more than you planned.

grammars.title: Imperatives you need to recognize
body: The true form comes from the future by dropping the prefix. Just three forms: to a man, to a woman, to a group.
after: ⚠️ **שְׁמַע** is the first word of the best-known Jewish prayer (שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל), and also the everyday word for "hey, listen" — a sentence opener Israelis use dozens of times a day. One word, two worlds.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Israelis speak far more directly than many visitors are used to**, and it isn't rudeness. Sentences like תֵּן לִי ("give me") or בּוֹא הֵנָּה ("come here") sound blunt in literal translation, but in Israel they're neutral. On the other hand, too much small talk can sound insincere. What people really notice isn't how long your sentence is but your **tone of voice**.
**כָּל הַכָּבוֹד** literally "all the honor" is used to praise someone's effort. When you finish this module and speak Hebrew with Israelis, it's the phrase you're most likely to hear.

sections.title: Shabbat: one day that shapes the whole week

blocks.text: You can't understand the rhythm of Israeli life without understanding שַׁבָּת. This isn't just a religious note — it decides when buses run, when shops open and when people invite you to eat.

items: **Shabbat starts at sunset on Friday** and ends on Saturday evening. Because the Jewish day starts in the evening, Friday evening already counts as Saturday.
**Friday-night dinner (אֲרוּחַת שַׁבָּת)** is the center of the Israeli family week, even for completely secular families. Being invited is a sign of closeness.
**Greetings used**: שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם from Friday midday to Saturday evening, then שָׁבוּעַ טוֹב ("good week") afterward.
**Closed**: almost all shops, public transport, offices. **Open**: restaurants and cafés in Tel Aviv and other big cities, beaches, parks and most tourist sites.

blocks.title: Greetings for special days
items: **שָׁבוּעַ טוֹב** — have a good week (Saturday evening).
**חַג שָׂמֵחַ** *(khag same'akh)* — happy holiday, for any festival.
**שָׁנָה טוֹבָה** *(shanah tovah)* — happy new year, used at Rosh Hashanah.
**בְּתֵאָבוֹן** — enjoy your meal, before eating together.
